lo:g10m10s2-1-2 'Use the mean and median of a continuous data set to judge whether the data meet a stated requirement, recognising that a mode usually cannot be computed for continuous data.': only finder B found it
median: not in the Egyptian Prep-3 maths book's vocabulary
mode: not in the Egyptian Prep-3 maths book's vocabulary
mean: Readers from other curricula (including the Egyptian national one) may know the mean as the average or the arithmetic mean; the book here says only mean.
continuous data: not in the Egyptian Prep-3 maths book's vocabulary
outlier: Readers from other curricula may know this as an extreme value or an anomalous value; the book defines it as a value not typical of the rest of the set.

histogram: not in the Egyptian Prep-3 maths book's vocabulary

range: Here a range is a sub-range or interval of values used to group data; many curricula use 'range' only for the largest value minus the smallest, and call the groups 'class intervals' or 'classes'.

evidence.quote: we add up the measurements and divide by the number of measurements
we sort the numbers from lowest to highest and find the value in the middle

check.note: WE7 (a0069) computes the mean by 'add up and divide' and the median by sorting and taking the middle, then uses both to judge the supplier. That is s2-1-1's method used as a step.

evidence.quote: Calculate the mean of the first learners
To find the median, we need to sort the data set

check.note: WE8 (a0070) calculates the mean of the first learners and sorts the data to find the median, before and after the outlier. It uses s2-1-1's mean and median calculation (odd and even count) as the steps.

evidence.quote: They work out that the mean number of stones they have is 6
Find a set of five ages for which the mean age is

check.note: Ex10-2:6 and Ex10-2:10 (a0079, a0084) start from a given mean, plus a given mode and median in the second. Working backwards needs the mean, mode and median calculations from s2-1-1.

evidence.quote: Since each mass can be represented by a number, the data set is quantitative.
we can usually not compute the mode of a continuous data set

check.note: a0069 classifies the data as quantitative and continuous, and on that basis says the mode cannot be computed. a0063 ('we can usually not compute the mode of a continuous data set') rests on knowing what continuous data is.

evidence.quote: each datum is treated as if it occurred at the centre of the range in which it was placed
calculate the mean, the modal group and the median group

check.note: a0101 says grouping changes the measures of central tendency, which recalls the ungrouped mean, median and mode. Ex10-4:1 (a0115) asks for the mean, modal group and median group, the grouped versions of s2-1-1's measures.

evidence.quote: remember that there are problems with computing the mode of continuous quantitative data
This is actually a better estimate of the mode

check.note: a0098 says 'remember that there are problems with computing the mode of continuous quantitative data', a direct refer-back to s2-1-2's mode clause. a0102 ('a better estimate of the mode') builds on that. The link is narrow but it is a genuine refer-back.

evidence.quote: Looking back to the previous worked example
After grouping the data, we now have the data set shown below

check.note: a0099 works from the result of grouping: values placed at range centres, repeated by the counts in each range, which is s3-1-1's frequency table. a0095 ('Looking back to the previous worked example') only points back, without saying which example.

evidence.quote: The histogram below shows the number of passengers that travel in Alfred
Calculate: an estimate of the mean

check.note: Ex10-4:3 (a0118, a0119) gives a histogram, and the student must read the counts off it to find the total and then an estimate of the mean. That is s3-1-2's histogram reading used as a step.

evidence.quote: It may be helpful for you to draw a histogram in order to answer the question.
Help them find which of the following data sets match the above histogram

check.note: Ex10-3:3 (a0107) says drawing a histogram may help count the values in a range, which uses s3-1-1's histogram construction. Ex10-3:7 (a0111) asks to match data sets to a histogram, which needs grouping and counting.

evidence.quote: A common way of handling continuous quantitative data is to subdivide the full range of values into a few sub-ranges
the data set changes from continuous to discrete

check.note: a0088 introduces grouping for 'continuous quantitative data' and says the grouped set 'changes from continuous to discrete'. That relies on the quantitative and discrete/continuous classification from s1-1-1.

evidence.quote: We have already encountered three percentiles in this chapter
we always have to order the values from the smallest to the largest

check.note: a0144 says the median was 'already encountered' and defined as the halfway value of a sorted set. a0160 requires ordering the data first, then finds the median. Both rest on s2-1-1's median and sorting.

evidence.quote: we still use the percentile formula to determine the rank of the percentile
Using the percentile formula and the fact that there are

check.note: a0153 says 'we still use the percentile formula to determine the rank' for grouped data, and a0162 applies the formula to find the rank. Both explicitly reuse s4-1-2's method.

evidence.quote: We have already encountered the full data range

check.note: a0156 says 'We have already encountered the full data range' (maximum minus minimum) while introducing ranges defined by percentiles. That is a refer-back to s4-1-1's range.

evidence.quote: calculated by subtracting the first quartile
Find the range, quartiles and the interquartile range.

check.note: a0157 defines the IQR as Q3 minus Q1, and Ex10-5:5 (a0167) asks for quartiles then the IQR. Finding the quartiles uses s4-1-2's method.

evidence.quote: the minimum value, the maximum value and the three quartiles
Using the percentile formula, we can determine that the median lies between the sixth and seventh values

check.note: a0177 defines the five number summary as the minimum, maximum and three quartiles (percentiles). a0180 finds the median and quartiles using the percentile formula and halving between two values, which is s4-1-2's method.

evidence.quote: This provides the five number summary of the data set and allows us to draw the following box-and-whisker plot
The box-and-whisker plot shows these five percentiles

check.note: a0180 says the five number summary 'allows us to draw the following box-and-whisker plot'. a0178 says the plot shows these five percentiles. Drawing the plot uses the summary as its input.

evidence.quote: numerically in the case of the five number summary and graphically in the case of the box-and-whisker plot
Determine the five number summary for each of the box-and-whisker plots below.

check.note: a0176 says the five number summary and the box-and-whisker plot hold the same information, one numerical and one graphical. Ex10-6:4a (a0184) asks for the five number summary from a plot, so it relies on the concept from s5-1-1.

evidence.quote: Round your answer to 1 decimal place
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

check.note: Ex10-2:1 (a0071) and WE7 (a0069) both require rounding the calculated mean to 1 decimal place. That uses the rounding skill described in g10m1s4-1-1 as a step.

dropped.reason: The range lesson uses the idea of an outlier, introduced and defined in 10.2, to explain how removing one value changes the range.

evidence.quote: The range is very sensitive to outliers.
It is an outlier and has a big influence on the range.

check.note: a0129 and a0159 only use the word 'outlier' (a0159 explains it in place as 'not typical'). Neither recalls or uses the s2-1-3 comparison of mean and median with and without an outlier. A shared word is not enough.
